Field Notes

Trail Finds

Fungi, moths, a caterpillar, and one spider's architecture, spotted along the same stretch of woods. Identifications below are best-effort visual calls, not lab-confirmed — several of these groups (jelly fungi, small orange mushrooms, geometer moths) are genuinely difficult to pin to an exact species from a photo alone.

Fungus

Orange Jelly Fungus

Dacrymyces chrysospermus

A bright orange-yellow, brain-like gelatinous fungus found on dead conifer wood. It swells up firm and glossy after rain and shrivels to a dark, crusty film in dry weather, only to rehydrate the next time it rains — the same fruiting body can do this many times over a season. Sometimes called “witch’s butter,” though that name gets applied loosely to several unrelated jelly fungi. Not toxic, but not worth eating either — mostly water and not much flavor.

Closest look-alike is Tremella mesenterica (true “yellow brain”), which grows on hardwood rather than conifer and has a more ruffled, brain-fold shape rather than smooth lobes.

Fungus

Witch’s Butter

Exidia sp., glandulosa group

A dusky purple-brown jelly fungus growing directly from the bark of a dead hardwood branch, in the same rubbery, shape-shifting family as the orange jelly fungus above but a different genus entirely. Fresh specimens are often this warm brown-purple; older ones darken toward black, which is where the “black witch’s butter” common name comes from. Feels like a firm gumdrop when fresh, shrinks to a dark flake in dry weather.

Exidia is a notoriously difficult genus to pin to species from a photo alone — several look-alikes (E. glandulosa, E. nigricans, E. plana) overlap heavily and reliable separation usually needs a microscope.

Caterpillar

American Dagger Moth (caterpillar)

Acronicta americana

Dense pale yellow-white fur with long black “pencil” tufts projecting from both the head and tail end, plus a couple of shorter black tufts along the back. This is a larval stage — it will pupate and emerge as a grey, fairly unremarkable-looking dagger moth. Feeds on the leaves of maples, oaks, sycamores, and other broadleaf trees.

Handle with care, not fingers — the fine hairs (setae) on many tussock and dagger moth caterpillars can cause a stinging skin reaction in sensitive people.

Moth

Fall Webworm Moth

Hyphantria cunea

A small, all-white, fuzzy-bodied moth — the adult form of the caterpillar responsible for the silky communal webs seen wrapped around the ends of tree branches in late summer. The moths themselves are harmless and short-lived; it's the gregarious caterpillar stage that does the tent-building.

Moth

Geometer Moth

family Geometridae

A small moth with soft, pale blue-grey wings held close over the body in a narrow triangle at rest — a classic resting posture for the geometer moths, the family whose caterpillars are the familiar “inchworms.” The plain, unmarked wings make an exact species call difficult from a photo alone; this family has thousands of similar-looking members.

Best read as a family-level ID rather than a confirmed species — genuinely hard to narrow further without a clearer wing-pattern shot.

Spider architecture

Funnel Web

likely Agelenidae (funnel weavers / grass spiders)

Not a mushroom or lichen — this is silk. A flat sheet of webbing spun across leaf litter and bark at the base of a trunk, narrowing into a funnel-shaped retreat that disappears into a crevice. The spider that built it waits inside the funnel and rushes out the moment a vibration on the sheet tells it something has landed. No spider was visible in the shot — it was almost certainly tucked deep in the tunnel.

Fungus

Golden Trumpets

likely Xeromphalina campanella

Tiny bright orange mushrooms with wiry, dark reddish-orange stems, growing in a tight cluster straight out of well-rotted, mossy wood. The scale is small — each cap is only about the width of a pencil eraser. Xeromphalina campanella typically fruits on decaying conifer logs and stumps, often in troops or dense clusters just like this one.

Small orange-capped mushrooms are one of the hardest groups to call precisely from a photo — several genera (Xeromphalina, Mycena, Gymnopus) converge on this same look, and a confident species ID usually needs a spore print.

Not a foraging guide — identifications here are for curiosity, not for eating anything pictured.
